title: Migration Should Not Be a Death Sentence: From San Fernando to Ciudad Juárez
author: Luis Eugenio Parés Sevilla

**The lives Mexico was supposed to protect.**

## From San Fernando to Ciudad Juárez: memory, routes, and pending
responsibilities.

Mexico is a territory of transit, but also of death. Two massacres of
migrants, separated by thirteen years, reveal a disturbing pattern: the State
responds with laws and promises, but the structure that produces the deaths
remains intact.

In August 2010, 72 migrants were murdered in San Fernando, Tamaulipas. On
March 27, 2023, another 40 died in a fire at a National Migration Institute
(INM) facility in Ciudad Juárez. These are different cases: one a massacre
attributed to Los Zetas, the other involving deaths in a fire while in state
custody. Both raise the question of who was responsible for protecting them
and what safeguards exist to prevent another tragedy.

Yes, there were institutional changes. In 2013, a Forensic Commission was
created with the participation of authorities, independent specialists, and
family organizations to identify victims of the San Fernando massacre and
other massacres. Mechanisms were also established for reporting crimes and
seeking information from abroad. However, the Foundation for Justice continued
to report nine unidentified victims out of the 72 and unanswered questions
about potential state responsibility. The convictions of members of the
criminal group do not complete the investigation.

![Migration Should Not Be a Death Sentence: From San Fernando to Ciudad
Juárez](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-06-body-p26.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

After Ciudad Juárez, the National Migration Institute (INM) temporarily
suspended operations at 33 detention centers and announced civil protection
upgrades. The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) documented serious
violations due to acts and omissions by its personnel. But inspecting
buildings alone does not solve the problem of a detention system: effective
evacuation, independent oversight, and clear accountability are also needed.
On October 13, 2026, a judge dismissed the case against former commissioner
Francisco Garduño, considering the conditions for suspending the proceedings
to have been met; representatives of the victims announced they would appeal.
That ruling does not clarify all the responsibilities for the fire.

The contrast is key. San Fernando produced laws, but it has not produced truth
or full justice. Ciudad Juárez, on the other hand, did not even produce a real
reform of the National Migration Institute (INM); the promised replacement of
the institute remained just talk. The immigration detention centers, far from
becoming spaces of protection, operated in fact as prisons under a policy of
containment and militarization.

Fifteen years later, the equation repeats itself: some perpetrators are
punished, but institutional responsibility is diluted. The families continue
searching, the nameless bodies continue waiting, and the central question
remains unanswered: who is responsible when the State is the custodian and
death occurs under its watch?

Meanwhile, the caravans are changing. In October 2026, groups of families from
Honduras, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua were documented; some were
seeking to settle and work in Mexico. Traveling together allows for sharing
aid and gaining visibility, but it doesn't guarantee safety. Documentation
delays also fuel these movements. The response must link regularization and
international protection, depending on the case, with safe transportation,
prevention of extortion, and funding for shelters. The assistance provided by
churches and organizations needs sustained public support.

![Migration Should Not Be a Death Sentence: From San Fernando to Ciudad
Juárez](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-
nov26-06-body-p27.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk About Migration_, November
2026

Returning to Mexico demands a similar responsibility. “México te Abraza”
(Mexico Embraces You) offers repatriated Mexican nationals’ documentation,
housing, transportation, healthcare, and job placement. Its evaluation must go
beyond simply providing services: how many people retain employment, find
housing, and receive psychological support months later? Federal, state, and
municipal governments need to coordinate follow-up. Foreign nationals deported
to Mexico require differentiated protection and documentation services.

The disappearance traces a geography that crosses Darién, Mexico, the Rio
Grande, Sonora, the Caribbean, the Mediterranean, and the Atlantic toward the
Canary Islands. The trail can be lost in a jungle, a kidnapping, a shipwreck,
or among disconnected institutional records. In Mexico, search commissions,
prosecutors' offices, forensic services, and consulates must coordinate;
internationally, equivalent cooperation is needed. The IOM warns that
restricting regular routes displaces migration toward more dangerous paths.

How many more tragedies does Mexico need to stop managing migrant suffering
and take responsibility? No apology can replace justice, and no compensation
guarantees that no one will die in detention again. We demand an investigation
into the entire chain of responsibility, that those responsible be punished,
and that a protection policy be funded that includes timely documentation,
safe transit, dignified shelters, and immediate search and rescue operations.

Remembering involves identifying, investigating, repairing, and preventing.
Success cannot be measured solely by how many people were contained or
returned; it must include how many were able to reach their destination,
remain in the country, or return alive and with their rights intact. No family
should have to travel to another country to demonstrate that the life of the
person they are searching for matters.

Dignity is not demonstrated with speeches, it is guaranteed with decisions,
budget and accountability.
